claim: The brainstem's lateral superior olive (LSO) is thought to be crucial for localizing high-frequency sounds by coding interaural sound level differences (ILD).
source: The brainstem's lateral superior olive (LSO) is thought to be crucial for localizing high-frequency sounds by coding interaural sound level differences (ILD).
evidence: This is a statement about the established role of LSO in sound localization, supported by citation to review literature (Tollin, 2003) in the Introduction.

claim: LSO neurons weigh contralateral inhibition against ipsilateral excitation, making their firing rate a function of the azimuthal position of a sound source.
source: Its neurons weigh contralateral inhibition against ipsilateral excitation, making their firing rate a function of the azimuthal position of a sound source.
evidence: This describes the computational mechanism of LSO neurons, which is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Since the very first in vivo recordings, LSO principal neurons have been reported to give sustained and temporally integrating 'chopper' responses to sustained sounds.
source: Since the very first in vivo recordings, LSO principal neurons have been reported to give sustained and temporally integrating 'chopper' responses to sustained sounds.
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical literature (e.g., Guinan et al., 1972a, 1972b; Tsuchitani, 1977) mentioned in the Introduction.

claim: Neurons with transient responses were observed but largely ignored and even considered a sign of pathology.
source: Neurons with transient responses were observed but largely ignored and even considered a sign of pathology.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the Discussion section (Tsuchitani and Johnson, 1991; Boudreau and Tsuchitani, 1970).

claim: Principal LSO neurons are the most numerous projection neurons of the LSO nucleus.
source: These results provide a new framework to interpret previously puzzling features of this circuit.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Saint Marie et al., 1989.

claim: Principal LSO neurons only respond at sound onset.
source: we have obtained the first in vivo patch clamp recordings from labeled LSO neurons and find that principal LSO neurons, the most numerous projection neurons of this nucleus, only respond at sound onset
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5, 6, and 8.

claim: Principal LSO neurons show fast membrane features suggesting an importance for timing.
source: we have obtained the first in vivo patch clamp recordings from labeled LSO neurons and find that principal LSO neurons, the most numerous projection neurons of this nucleus, only respond at sound onset and show fast membrane features suggesting an importance for timing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing fast EPSPs and high upper cut-off frequencies.

claim: LSO neurons are sensitive to sound level differences between the ears (interaural level differences or ILD).
source: Its neurons are sensitive to sound level differences between the ears (interaural level differences or ILD; see Tollin, 2003, for review).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Tollin, 2003.

claim: Neurons in the LSO accomplish ILD sensitivity by weighing the sound input to the ipsilateral ear, conveyed via an excitatory (glutamatergic) projection from the ipsilateral cochlear nucleus, against the sound input to the contralateral ear, conveyed via an inhibitory (glycinergic) afferent from the homolateral medial nucleus of the trapezoid body.
source: Neurons in the LSO accomplish this by weighing the sound input to the ipsilateral ear, conveyed via an excitatory (glutamatergic) projection from the ipsilateral cochlear nucleus (Cant, 1991; Smith et al., 1993; Doucet and Ryugo, 2003), against the sound input to the contralateral ear, conveyed via an inhibitory (glycinergic) afferent from the homolateral medial nucleus of the trapezoid body (Figure 1A) (Glendenning et al., 1985; Banks and Smith, 1992; Sommer et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The ILD tuning process results in firing rates that vary monotonically with ILD.
source: This process results in firing rates that vary monotonically with ILD
evidence: This is established knowledge about LSO function.

claim: LSO ILD tuning is conveyed to targets in the midbrain: the ipsilateral and contralateral inferior colliculi (IC) and the contralateral dorsal nucleus of the lateral lemniscus (DNLL).
source: and this tuning is conveyed to targets in the midbrain: the ipsilateral and contralateral inferior colliculi (IC) and the contralateral dorsal nucleus of the lateral lemniscus (DNLL) (Glendenning and Masterton, 1983; Moore, 1988; Saint Marie et al., 1989; Glendenning et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing LSO projection targets.

claim: Reports based on extracellular recordings have consistently indicated that the majority of LSO neurons generate sustained 'chopper' responses to ipsilateral tones and thus temporally integrate auditory input.
source: Reports based on extracellular recordings have consistently indicated that the majority of LSO neurons generate sustained 'chopper' responses to ipsilateral tones and thus temporally integrate auditory input (e.g. Guinan et al., 1972a, 1972b; Tsuchitani, 1977; Greene and Davis, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple extracellular recording studies.

claim: The sustained chopper response feature is typically used as a physiological criterion to define LSO units.
source: Typically, this feature is used as a physiological criterion to define LSO units (e.g. Finlayson and Caspary, 1989; Joris and Yin, 1995; Tollin et al., 2008; Tsai et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies that used this criterion.

claim: At least 5 types of LSO neurons have been defined in cat and gerbil, based on dendritic configuration and the size, location and synaptic coverage of the cell body.
source: Morphologically, at least 5 types of LSO neurons have been defined in cat and gerbil, based on dendritic configuration and the size, location and synaptic coverage of the cell body (Helfert and Schwartz, 1986; 1987; Rietzel and Friauf, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to morphological studies.

claim: Seventy to eighty percent of LSO cells have a bipolar dendritic configuration.
source: Seventy to eighty percent of LSO cells have a bipolar dendritic configuration
evidence: This is based on cited morphological studies.

claim: The majority of bipolar LSO cells can be classified as principal cells with cell bodies displaying an extensive synaptic coverage.
source: The majority can be classified as principal cells with cell bodies displaying an extensive synaptic coverage
evidence: This is based on cited morphological studies and confirmed by the authors' EM data in Figure 3.

claim: A smaller percentage of bipolar cells have cell bodies that are sparsely innervated and are termed class 5 cells.
source: but the cell bodies of a smaller percentage of bipolar cells are sparsely innervated and termed class 5 cells.
evidence: This is based on cited morphological studies.

claim: Around 13% of the LSO cell population are classified as multiplanar cells, with multipolar dendritic trees and an extensive synaptic coverage of the cell body, or marginal cells, with multipolar or unipolar dendritic trees and sparsely innervated cell bodies that are situated along the margins of the body of the LSO neuropil.
source: Around 13% of the LSO cell population are classified as multiplanar cells, with multipolar dendritic trees and an extensive synaptic coverage of the cell body, or marginal cells, with multipolar or unipolar dendritic trees and sparsely innervated cell bodies that are situated along the margins of the body of the LSO neuropil.
evidence: This is based on cited morphological studies.

claim: The remaining LSO cells are classified as small, have very sparsely innervated cell bodies, and are thought to belong to the olivocochlear system.
source: The remaining LSO cells are classified as small, have very sparsely innervated cell bodies, and are thought to belong to the olivocochlear system (Radtke-Schuller et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Radtke-Schuller et al., 2015.

claim: Most LSO neurons that project to the inferior colliculus are principal cells.
source: A retrograde labeling study indicated that most LSO neurons that project to the inferior colliculus are principal cells (Saint Marie et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Saint Marie et al., 1989.

claim: It has been implicitly assumed that the most frequently observed response pattern (sustained response with a chopping pattern) is associated with principal cells.
source: Implicitly, it has been assumed that the most frequently observed response pattern, that is a sustained response with a chopping pattern, is associated with principal cells.
evidence: This is an inference about the field's assumptions based on the literature.

claim: In vitro slice studies have shown evidence for multiple response patterns in LSO cells in response to current injection.
source: In these studies as well, there is evidence for multiple response patterns in response to current injection, and debate regarding the meaning of these patterns and reasons for discrepancies between studies.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple in vitro studies.

claim: Non-olivocochlear LSO neurons were associated with both onset and sustained firing to depolarizing current, where the onset response seems to depend on the higher concentration of a low voltage-activated potassium channel (Kv1).
source: Non-olivocochlear LSO neurons were associated with both onset and sustained firing to depolarizing current, where the onset response seems to depend on the higher concentration of a low voltage-activated potassium channel (Kv1).
evidence: This is based on in vitro studies cited in the Introduction.

claim: In almost all in vitro studies, cells with onset and sustained firing properties were classified as 'principal' typically based on visualization of the cell body size and shape, and the presence of Ih current.
source: In almost all of these studies, cells with these onset and sustained firing properties were classified as 'principal' typically based on visualization of the cell body size and shape, and the presence of Ih current.
evidence: This is an observation about the methods used in cited in vitro studies.

claim: Only rarely was labeling done to verify the dendritic tree configuration in in vitro studies, and the synaptic coverage of the cell body was never evaluated.
source: Only rarely (Adam et al., 1999; Barnes-Davies et al., 2004) was labeling done to verify the dendritic tree configuration, and the synaptic coverage of the cell body was never evaluated.
evidence: This is an observation about the methods used in cited in vitro studies.

claim: Only one previously published report describes in vivo intracellular responses of cells localized to the LSO, in chinchilla.
source: Only one previously published report (Finlayson and Caspary, 1989) describes in vivo intracellular responses of cells localized to the LSO, in chinchilla.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Finlayson and Caspary, 1989.

claim: The Finlayson and Caspary study only describes cells with chopper responses to ipsilateral tones.
source: As with many of the extracellular reports, this paper only describes cells with chopper responses to ipsilateral tones.
evidence: This is based on citation to Finlayson and Caspary, 1989.

claim: In the Finlayson and Caspary study, two cells were labeled with Lucifer Yellow and classified as principal cells based on dendritic configuration but no electron microscopy was done.
source: Two cells were labeled with Lucifer Yellow and classified as principal cells based on dendritic configuration but no electron microscopy was done.
evidence: This is based on citation to Finlayson and Caspary, 1989.

claim: In almost all of the intracellular recordings reported in the Finlayson and Caspary study, ipsilateral acoustic stimuli at the cell's characteristic frequency generated 'robust' suprathreshold excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) while contralateral stimuli generated inhibitory postsynaptic potentials (IPSPs).
source: In almost all of the intracellular recordings reported in that study, ipsilateral acoustic stimuli at the cell's characteristic frequency (CF: frequency of lowest threshold) generated 'robust' suprathreshold excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) while contralateral stimuli generated inhibitory postsynaptic potentials (IPSPs).
evidence: This is based on citation to Finlayson and Caspary, 1989.

claim: In the few cases studied with binaural stimulation in the Finlayson and Caspary study, the inhibitory input was capable of suppressing the spike output generated by the ipsilaterally-evoked EPSPs.
source: In the few cases studied with binaural stimulation, the inhibitory input was capable of suppressing the spike output generated by the ipsilaterally-evoked EPSPs.
evidence: This is based on citation to Finlayson and Caspary, 1989.

claim: The authors obtained in vivo whole-cell recordings from 25 neurons in the gerbil LSO, of which 16 were labeled with biocytin.
source: We have obtained in vivo whole-cell recordings from 25 neurons in the gerbil LSO, of which 16 were labeled with biocytin (Supplementary file 1; example cell camera lucida reconstruction in Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data.

claim: For all recorded LSO cells, ipsilateral tones generated EPSPs and often action potentials.
source: For all cells, ipsilateral tones generated EPSPs and often action potentials (Figure 1C, blue trace).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In response to contralateral tones, IPSPs were elicited in all cases tested (including all unlabeled neurons).
source: In response to contralateral tones, IPSPs were elicited (Figure 1C, green trace) in all cases tested (including all unlabeled neurons).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: When sound was presented binaurally, the ipsilateral depolarization and ensuing spiking could be suppressed by the contralateral inhibition, generating sensitivity to ILD in all cases tested (including all unlabeled neurons).
source: When sound was presented binaurally, the ipsilateral depolarization and ensuing spiking could be suppressed by the contralateral inhibition (Figure 1C, black trace), generating sensitivity to ILD (Figure 1D) in all cases tested (including all unlabeled neurons).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: Light and electron microscopic analysis of labeled neurons allowed the authors to unambiguously identify five neurons as principal cells.
source: Light and electron microscopic analysis of labeled neurons allowed us to unambiguously identify five neurons as principal cells (Figure 2A, green symbols; Supplementary file 1, cells 1–5), using previously reported features for gerbil LSO neurons (Helfert and Schwartz, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 3, and by citation to Helfert and Schwartz, 1987.

claim: At the light microscopic level, principal cells have cell bodies located centrally in the LSO and bipolar dendritic arbors in the transverse plane.
source: At the light microscopic level, principal cells have cell bodies located centrally in the LSO and bipolar dendritic arbors in the transverse plane (Figure 2A, top row).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and by citation to Helfert and Schwartz, 1987.

claim: At the electron microscopic level, principal cells are characterized by high levels of cell body synaptic coverage.
source: At the electron microscopic (E.M.) level, principal cells are characterized by high levels of cell body synaptic coverage (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The authors identified seven non-principal LSO cells, which can be further subdivided in three groups.
source: In addition, we identified seven non-principal LSO cells, which can be further subdivided in three groups (Supplementary file 1, cells 10–16).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data.

claim: The authors identified one class 5 cell, which can only be distinguished from principal cells at the E.M. level by low cell body synaptic coverage.
source: We identified one class 5 cell, which can only be distinguished from principal cells at the E.M. level by low cell body synaptic coverage.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The authors identified five marginal cells with cell bodies located in the LSO marginal area.
source: Five other cells could be classified as marginal cells - these cell bodies were located in the LSO marginal area (Figure 2A, bottom row).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: E.M. analysis of 4 marginal cell bodies confirmed that they had synaptic coverage levels that fell well below those for gerbil principal cells.
source: E.M. analysis of 4 marginal cell bodies (Figure 3) confirmed that they had synaptic coverage levels that fell well below those for gerbil principal cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The authors identified one multiplanar cell, whose cell body was located in the body of the LSO and had a multipolar dendritic tree.
source: Finally, we identified one multiplanar cell, whose cell body was located in the body of the LSO and had a multipolar dendritic tree (Figure 2A, near figure center, cell 15).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The multiplanar cell had an extensive synaptic coverage of 75.3% that was consistent with the range of coverages reported by Helfert and Schwartz for this cell type.
source: This cell had an extensive synaptic coverage of 75.3% that was consistent with the range of coverages reported by Helfert and Schwartz (Helfert and Schwartz, 1987) for this cell type (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and by citation to Helfert and Schwartz, 1987.

claim: None of the authors' labeled cells had light and electron microscopic features corresponding to 'small' cells in gerbil LSO, most or all of which are thought to be part of the olivocochlear system.
source: None of our labeled cells had light and electron microscopic features corresponding to 'small' cells in gerbil LSO, most or all of which are thought to be part of the olivocochlear system (Radtke-Schuller et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental observations and supported by citation to Radtke-Schuller et al., 2015.

claim: CF or BF shows a clear increase to higher values towards the medial pole of the LSO nucleus.
source: CF or BF shows a clear increase to higher values towards the medial pole of the nucleus (Figure 2A/B), consistent with earlier extracellular recordings (e.g. Guinan et al., 1972b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and by citation to Guinan et al., 1972b.

claim: All four identified cell types conform to the tonotopic gradient in the LSO.
source: All four identified cell types conform to this tonotopic gradient.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In all LSO cell types, spontaneous synaptic activity consisted of excitatory (EPSPs) and inhibitory (IPSPs) postsynaptic potentials.
source: In all cell types, spontaneous synaptic activity consisted of excitatory (EPSPs: green dots) and inhibitory (IPSPs: red dots) postsynaptic potentials.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Principal cells were characterized by strikingly fast, narrow EPSPs.
source: We observed that principal cells were characterized by strikingly fast, narrow EPSPs (Figure 4A, left column).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: For principal cells EPSPs often had sub-millisecond half widths that are reminiscent of principal MSO cells.
source: Indeed, for principal cells EPSPs often had sub-millisecond half widths that are reminiscent of principal MSO cells (Figure 4B; compare with [Scott et al., 2005; Franken et al., 2015]).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and by citations to Scott et al., 2005 and Franken et al., 2015.

claim: EPSPs of non-principal cells were slower than those of principal cells.
source: In contrast, EPSPs of non-principal cells were slower (Figure 4A, right column).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Spontaneous activity of LSO principal cells contained a significantly larger proportion of high frequencies than that of LSO non-principal cells.
source: Spontaneous activity of LSO principal cells contained a significantly larger proportion of high frequencies than that of LSO non-principal cells (upper cut-off frequency was respectively 528.7 ± 66.5 and 131.4 ± 15.5 Hz; two-sample t test t10 = 6.83, p=4.6×10−5, Hedges' g = 4.00)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The upper cut-off frequency of spontaneous activity of LSO principal cells was similar to spectra of MSO principal cells.
source: and was similar to spectra of MSO principal cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Action potentials were smaller in principal cells than in non-principal cells and typically did not overshoot 0 mV.
source: We observed that action potentials were smaller in principal cells than in non-principal cells and typically did not overshoot 0 mV (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Principal neurons had an average action potential amplitude of 28.3 ± 5.2 mV, and non-principal neurons an average action potential amplitude of 66.3 ± 4.5 mV, a difference that was statistically significant.
source: This difference was significant across the population of labeled neurons: principal neurons had an average action potential amplitude of 28.3 ± 5.2 mV (mean ± s.e.m.), and non-principal neurons an average action potential amplitude of 66.3 ± 4.5 mV (two-tailed two-sample t test: t10 = −5.48, p=2.67×10−4, Hedges' g = 3.21).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The difference in action potential amplitude between principal cells and non-principal cells could not be explained by a systematic difference in bridge balance between the two cell types.
source: This difference could not be explained by a systematic difference in bridge balance between principal cells and non-principal cells (series resistance was 65.2 ± 6.4 MΩ for principal cells and 65.6 ± 8.1 MΩ for non-principal cells (mean ± s.e.m.), two sample t9 = −0.03, p=0.98).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Upper cut-off frequency of the spectrum of spontaneous membrane potential fluctuations and action potential amplitude cluster differently for morphologically confirmed principal cells and non-principal cells.
source: These two features, upper cut-off frequency of the spectrum of spontaneous membrane potential fluctuations and action potential amplitude, cluster differently for morphologically confirmed principal cells and non-principal cells (Figure 4E, compare green circles and black stars).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Ipsilateral tones generated strong onset responses in principal neurons.
source: Surprisingly, we found that ipsilateral tones generated strong onset responses in principal neurons (Figure 5, top)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Principal neurons never showed a sustained, chopping pattern in response to ipsilateral tones.
source: and never a sustained, chopping pattern, which is considered the canonical spiking pattern of LSO neurons (Tsuchitani, 1977; Joris and Yin, 1995; Tollin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and by citations to previous studies.

claim: Chopping firing patterns were restricted to non-principal neurons.
source: Instead, chopping firing patterns were restricted to non-principal neurons (Figure 5, bottom, e.g. cells 10, 14 and the cell with CF 3.2 kHz; Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Since none of the principal cells showed a chopper pattern or high level of sustained activity, the data imply that principal cells are severely underrepresented in the LSO literature.
source: Since none of the principal cells showed a chopper pattern or high level of sustained activity, our data imply that principal cells are severely underrepresented in the LSO literature, and that this literature builds on a biased selection of non-principal neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and comparison with the literature.

claim: All principal cells tested responded with an onset spike to depolarizing current injections, and offset spikes to hyperpolarizing responses.
source: We observed that all principal cells tested responded with an onset spike to depolarizing current injections, and offset spikes to hyperpolarizing responses (Figure 6A, top).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Non-principal cells were able to generate sustained responses to depolarizing current injections.
source: In contrast, non-principal cells were able to generate sustained responses to depolarizing current injections (Figure 6A, bottom).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The spike patterns to depolarizing current steps were strikingly similar to those elicited by ipsilateral tones for these neurons.
source: Furthermore, the spike patterns to depolarizing current steps were strikingly similar to those elicited by ipsilateral tones for these neurons (Figure 6B, compare with Figure 6A)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: Principal cells are characterized by onset firing, which relates to the intrinsic properties of the neuron, as it can be found not only to auditory stimuli but also to depolarizing current steps.
source: We conclude that principal cells are characterized by onset firing, which relates to the intrinsic properties of the neuron, as it can be found not only to auditory stimuli but also to depolarizing current steps.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Principal MSO neurons also respond with a single onset spike to depolarizing current steps.
source: Again, this is a feature reminiscent of principal MSO neurons, which also respond with a single onset spike to depolarizing current steps (e.g. Scott et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Scott et al., 2005.

claim: A voltage sag indicative of Ih current was observed in response to hyperpolarizing current pulses in all neurons regardless of type.
source: In response to hyperpolarizing current pulses we observed a voltage sag indicative of Ih current in all neurons regardless of type (Figure 6A; note that the principal cell shown in the second row also generated such a sag, visible in a separate dataset with adjusted bridge balance (not shown)).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Both principal cells had a lower input resistance than the non-principal cells for which input resistance could be calculated.
source: We could calculate the input resistance at the peak and steady state of the voltage response to hyperpolarizing current in two principal cells and three non-principal cells: both principal cells had a lower input resistance than the non-principal cells (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data reported in Supplementary file 1.

claim: In all labeled LSO neurons, ipsilateral tones evoked mainly EPSPs and contralateral sounds evoked mainly IPSPs.
source: In all labeled LSO neurons, ipsilateral tones evoked mainly EPSPs and contralateral sounds evoked mainly IPSPs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The response of principal cells to contralateral stimulation showed a pronounced peak (in the hyperpolarization direction) at sound onset, and a much smaller hyperpolarization during the sustained part of the response.
source: As was the case for responses to ipsilateral stimulation, the response of principal cells to contralateral stimulation also showed a pronounced peak (but in the hyperpolarization direction) at sound onset, and a much smaller hyperpolarization during the sustained part of the response (Figure 7; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The latency of the inhibitory onset response decreases by several ms with increasing sound level.
source: The latency of the inhibitory onset response decreases by several ms with increasing sound level (see next section).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Non-principal cells typically show postsynaptic potentials with larger amplitudes, often with a more sluggish onset, compared to principal cells.
source: By comparison non-principal cells typically show postsynaptic potentials with larger amplitudes (Figure 7; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B), often with a more sluggish onset.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Non-principal cells had significantly smaller peak-to-sustained postsynaptic amplitude ratios than principal cells, during monaural ipsilateral as well as monaural contralateral stimulation.
source: These differences resulted in significantly smaller peak-to-sustained postsynaptic amplitude ratios for non-principal cells than for principal cells, during monaural ipsilateral as well as monaural contralateral stimulation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C; resp. two-tailed t-test t10 = 2.24; p=0.049 and t10 = 3.02; p=0.013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: For the inhibitory responses, non-principal cells are more integrative than principal cells.
source: Thus, also for the inhibitory responses, non-principal cells are more integrative than principal cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The evoked spike rate during ipsilateral sound stimulation correlated with the amplitude of hyperpolarization during contralateral sound stimulation.
source: Excitatory and inhibitory responses were matched in the sense that the evoked spike rate during ipsilateral sound stimulation correlated with the amplitude of hyperpolarization during contralateral sound stimulation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D; r = −0.64; p=0.035).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The amplitude of both excitatory and inhibitory potentials typically increased with sound level.
source: The amplitude of both excitatory and inhibitory potentials typically increased with sound level (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The relation of postsynaptic potential amplitude to sound level was often non-monotonic, where the amplitude decreased again for the highest sound levels.
source: The relation to sound level was often non-monotonic, where the amplitude decreased again for the highest sound levels (Figure 7B; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The non-monotonicity in sound level response may reflect acoustic crosstalk.
source: The sound level at which the non-monotonicity occurred, as well as the observation that the non-monotonicity is mirror-symmetric for ipsi- and contralateral stimulation, suggest that it may reflect acoustic crosstalk.
evidence: This is speculation based on experimental observations and comparison with Wei et al., 2017.

claim: In neurons with non-monotonic responses, IPSPs could be observed to high-level ipsilateral tones.
source: Indeed, in neurons with non-monotonic responses, IPSPs could be observed to high-level ipsilateral tones (Figure 7—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: EPSPs could be observed to high level contralateral tones in neurons with non-monotonic responses.
source: and EPSPs to high level contralateral tones (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Another possible mechanism for the non-monotonic response to ipsilateral stimulation is ipsilateral inhibition, which has been reported in vitro and was also inferred from in vivo observations of inhibitory sidebands.
source: Another possible mechanism for the non-monotonic response to ipsilateral stimulation is ipsilateral inhibition, which has been reported in vitro (Wu and Kelly, 1994) and was also inferred from in vivo observations of inhibitory sidebands (Brownell et al., 1979; Caird and Klinke, 1983).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to Wu and Kelly, 1994; Brownell et al., 1979; Caird and Klinke, 1983.

claim: The intracellular responses show that the non-monotonicity reflects neural interaction at the site of LSO neurons, and is not simply a reflection of the non-monotonicity that can be found in the monaural inputs to LSO neurons.
source: In any case, the intracellular responses show that the non-monotonicity reflects neural interaction at the site of LSO neurons, and is not simply a reflection of the (more modest) non-monotonicity that can be found in the monaural inputs to LSO neurons (Wei et al., 2017; Kopp-Scheinpflug et al., 2002; Kuenzel et al., 2011; Typlt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data and comparison with cited studies.

claim: The latency of the EPSP evoked by the ipsilateral tone at 50 dB is similar to that of the IPSP evoked by a contralateral tone of the same SPL in a principal cell.
source: The latency of the EPSP evoked by the ipsilateral tone at 50 dB is similar to that of the IPSP evoked by a contralateral tone of the same SPL
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: When ipsilateral and contralateral tones at the same SPL are combined (ILD = 0 dB), they interact to a response that fails to elicit a spike in a principal cell.
source: and when combined (ILD = 0 dB), they interact to a response that fails to elicit a spike.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: At a contralateral sound level of 30 dB (ILD = −20 dB), the contralateral IPSP arrives too late to be able to suppress the ipsilateral excitation evoked by a 50 dB tone in a principal cell.
source: However, at a contralateral sound level of 30 dB (ILD = −20 dB), the contralateral IPSP arrives simply too late to be able to suppress the ipsilateral excitation evoked by a 50 dB tone.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Because non-principal neurons have slower PSPs and sustained responses to ipsi- and contralateral sound, their spike output is less dependent on the exact timing of PSPs.
source: Because non-principal neurons have slower PSPs (Figure 4) and sustained responses to ipsi- and contralateral sound, their spike output is less dependent on the exact timing of PSPs
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 8.

claim: ILD-sensitivity in non-principal neurons can extend throughout the stimulus duration.
source: and ILD-sensitivity can extend throughout the stimulus duration.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Both principal and non-principal cells contribute to ILD-sensitivity at sound onset.
source: A population analysis of ILD functions reveals indeed that both principal and non-principal cells contribute to ILD-sensitivity at sound onset (Figure 9A)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Principal cells do not contribute to ILD sensitivity beyond the first 10 ms.
source: but that principal cells do not contribute to ILD sensitivity beyond the first 10 ms (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: No significant differences were observed between principal cells and non-principal cells in terms of position of the slope of the ILD function.
source: We did not observe significant differences between principal cells and non-principal cells in terms of position of the slope of the ILD function (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No significant differences were observed between principal cells and non-principal cells in terms of the range of ILDs covered by the slope.
source: or of the range of ILDs covered by the slope (Figure 9—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Higher ipsilateral sound levels can move the slope of the ILD function towards more negative ILDs.
source: we find that higher ipsilateral sound levels can move the slope of the ILD function towards more negative ILDs, as has been previously reported (Figure 9—figure supplement 2; Park et al., 2004; Tsuchitani and Boudreau, 1969; Tsai et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2 and by citations to Park et al., 2004; Tsuchitani and Boudreau, 1969; Tsai et al., 2010.

claim: For 8 cells, the axon could be followed to the point where the authors were confident about whether they projected to the ipsilateral or contralateral inferior colliculus.
source: For 8 cells, we could follow the axon to the point where we were confident about whether they projected to the ipsilateral or contralateral inferior colliculus (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental observations.

claim: The three traceable principal cell axons all headed ipsilaterally as did three non-principal cells.
source: The three traceable principal cell axons all headed ipsilaterally as did three non-principal cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data reported in Supplementary file 1.

claim: One non-principal cell headed contralaterally and another one projected bilaterally, bifurcating just after exiting the LSO dorsally.
source: One other non-principal cell headed contralaterally and another one projected bilaterally, bifurcating just after exiting the LSO dorsally.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data reported in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Two labeled principal and one non-principal neuron, all of which projected to the ipsilateral inferior colliculus and are thus probably glycinergic, sent an axon collateral to the ipsilateral lateral nucleus of the trapezoid body (LNTB).
source: In addition, two labeled principal and one non-principal neuron, all of which projected to the ipsilateral inferior colliculus and are thus probably glycinergic, sent an axon collateral to the ipsilateral lateral nucleus of the trapezoid body (LNTB; one of these cells has been reported before [Franken et al., 2016]).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10 and by citation to Franken et al., 2016.

claim: Three non-principal neurons had local axon collaterals in the LSO.
source: Three non-principal neurons had local axon collaterals in the LSO (Figure 10 and Supplementary Text).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10.

claim: The data do not support a simple dichotomy between principal and non-principal cells in laterality of projections to the midbrain or superior olivary complex.
source: In summary, the data do not support a simple dichotomy between principal and non-principal cells in laterality of projections to the midbrain or superior olivary complex.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data about axonal projections.

claim: The monaural and binaural responses to tones suggest an important functional difference for principal and non-principal neurons.
source: Taken together, the monaural and binaural responses to tones (Figures 4–9) suggest an important functional difference for principal and non-principal neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figures 4–9.

claim: Non-principal neurons integrate over time and enable the coding of ILDs of sustained sounds.
source: Non-principal neurons integrate over time and enable the coding of ILDs of sustained sounds.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figures 4–9.

claim: Principal neurons are differentiators that are particularly sensitive to timing aspects of the sound stimulus such as stimulus onset, but lack sensitivity to sustained parts of the stimulus.
source: Principal neurons are differentiators that are particularly sensitive to timing aspects of the sound stimulus such as stimulus onset, but lack sensitivity to sustained parts of the stimulus.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figures 4–9.

claim: The findings confirm the morphological classes discerned in gerbil LSO by Helfert and Schwartz, 1987.
source: Our findings confirm the morphological classes discerned in this species (Helfert and Schwartz, 1987) and allow us to link these to physiology.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3 and by citation to Helfert and Schwartz, 1987.

claim: All four large LSO cell types are excited by sounds to the ipsilateral ear and inhibited by sounds to the contralateral ear.
source: We present the first evidence that all these cell types are excited by sounds to the ipsilateral ear and inhibited by sounds to the contralateral ear
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 7.

claim: All four large LSO cell types conform to the tonotopic LSO map.
source: and that they conform to the tonotopic LSO map.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Principal LSO cells do not show the prototypical integrative chopper responses that have been attributed to these cells since the earliest single-cell studies.
source: Unexpectedly and most importantly, our data reveal that principal LSO cells do not show the prototypical integrative chopper responses that have been attributed to these cells since the earliest single-cell studies
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Principal LSO cells display fast kinetics and onset responses.
source: rather, they display fast kinetics and onset responses
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4, 5, and 6.

claim: The findings necessitate a revision of the prevailing notion of LSO as a high-frequency nucleus integrating auditory information over time to send ILD cues to higher centers in the brain.
source: which necessitates a revision of the prevailing notion of LSO as a high-frequency nucleus integrating auditory information over time to send ILD cues to higher centers in the brain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and their implications for understanding LSO function.

claim: Axons of several principal and non-principal cells could be followed into the ipsilateral or contralateral lateral lemniscus indicating that these different cell types are olivocollicular.
source: Axons of several principal and non-principal cells could be followed into the ipsilateral or contralateral lateral lemniscus (LL) indicating that these different cell types are olivocollicular.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data reported in Supplementary file 1.

claim: LSO principal cells provide a computational nexus in parallel to MSO principal cells.
source: LSO principal cells provide a computational nexus in parallel to MSO principal cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and comparison with MSO.

claim: Traditionally, LSO and MSO circuits are thought to mainly provide high-frequency ILD and low-frequency ITD information, respectively, to higher centers.
source: Traditionally, these two circuits are thought to mainly provide high-frequency ILD and low-frequency ITD information, respectively, to higher centers.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: MSO cells sense microsecond differences in arrival time using ILVK and Ih currents that lead to low input resistance, fast postsynaptic potentials and onset spikes to depolarizing current injection.
source: MSO cells sense microsecond differences in arrival time using ILVK and Ih currents that lead to low input resistance, fast postsynaptic potentials and onset spikes to depolarizing current injection (Scott et al., 2005; Mathews et al., 2010; Khurana et al., 2011; Franken et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Scott et al., 2005; Mathews et al., 2010; Khurana et al., 2011; Franken et al., 2015.

claim: LSO neurons are biased to high frequencies, where ongoing temporal cues are less dominant.
source: LSO neurons are biased to high frequencies, where ongoing temporal cues are less dominant.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: LSO principal cells have several properties reminiscent of MSO principal cells.
source: We show that LSO principal cells have several properties reminiscent of MSO principal cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 6.

claim: LSO principal cells display smaller spikes than non-principal cells.
source: They display smaller spikes than non-principal cells
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: LSO principal cells consistently fire onset spikes to positive current injection.
source: and consistently fire onset spikes to positive current injection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Firing patterns evoked by sustained auditory stimuli mirror responses evoked by current injection in LSO cells.
source: Firing patterns evoked by sustained auditory stimuli mirror responses evoked by current injection
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Principal cells generate an onset spike to sustained tones, unlike non-principal cells which typically fire throughout the stimulus duration.
source: principal cells generate an onset spike to sustained tones, unlike non-principal cells which typically fire throughout the stimulus duration.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The difference in spiking activity between principal and non-principal cells was accompanied by contrasting postsynaptic potential profiles with mainly onset responses in principal cells and more sustained activity in non-principal cells.
source: This difference in spiking activity was accompanied by contrasting postsynaptic potential profiles with mainly onset responses in principal cells and more sustained activity in non-principal cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 7.

claim: The properties of LSO principal cells are inconsistent with the prevailing view that LSO principal cells integrate auditory stimulation over time by generating sustained, chopping responses to tones.
source: These are unexpected properties that are inconsistent with the prevailing view that LSO principal cells integrate auditory stimulation over time by generating sustained, chopping responses to tones.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and comparison with the literature.

claim: The traditional association of ILD-sensitive neurons in LSO with chopper responses emerged from pioneering studies in the cat reporting the first single-cell recordings.
source: The traditional association of ILD-sensitive neurons in LSO with chopper responses, which has stood for 50 years, emerged from pioneering studies in the cat reporting the first single-cell recordings (Tsuchitani and Boudreau, 1966, 1968, Boudreau and Tsuchitani, 1970; Guinan et al., 1972a, 1972b; Tsuchitani, 1977).
evidence: This is supported by citations to early studies.

claim: Early studies found chopper responses to be the most frequently observed in LSO.
source: Not only did these early studies find chopper responses to be the most frequently observed
evidence: This is supported by citations to early studies.

claim: Phasic and transient responses in LSO were considered outright pathological in early studies.
source: phasic and transient responses were considered outright pathological (Tsuchitani and Johnson, 1991; Boudreau and Tsuchitani, 1970).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tsuchitani and Johnson, 1991; Boudreau and Tsuchitani, 1970.

claim: The view that phasic responses were pathological biased the ensuing literature on LSO.
source: This point of view biased the ensuing literature.
evidence: This is an inference based on the historical development of the field.

claim: In later studies, the presence of ILD-sensitive choppers in LSO was confirmed, not only in cat but also in other species.
source: In later studies, the presence of ILD-sensitive choppers in LSO was confirmed, not only in cat (Caird and Klinke, 1983; Joris and Yin, 1995; Tollin et al., 2002; Greene and Davis, 2012) but also in other species, for example in chinchilla (Finlayson and Caspary, 1989), rat (Irvine et al., 2001), bat (Harnischfeger et al., 1985), and gerbil (Sanes and Rubel, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The chopper response came to be seen as a signature property of LSO, even though a minority of other response types was also reported, including transient responses.
source: The chopper response came to be seen as a signature property, even though a minority of other response types was also reported, including transient responses.
evidence: This is an observation about the field's interpretation of the literature.

claim: Because the principal cells are the most numerous cells in LSO, it was reasonable to assume that these cells produce the most frequently encountered response type, that is chopping.
source: Because the principal cells are the most numerous cells in LSO, it was reasonable to assume that these cells produce the most frequently encountered response type, that is chopping.
evidence: This is an inference about the field's reasoning.

claim: In none of the studies reporting chopper responses was single-cell labeling attempted, except in one study in chinchilla.
source: In none of these studies, however, was single-cell labeling attempted, except in one study in chinchilla (Finlayson and Caspary, 1989).
evidence: This is an observation about the methods used in cited studies.

claim: In the Finlayson and Caspary study, the initial assumption was that LSO principal cells displayed chopper responses to ipsilateral stimuli.
source: Again, in this study the initial assumption was that '… LSO principal cells … displayed chopper responses to ipsilateral stimuli'.
evidence: This is based on citation to Finlayson and Caspary, 1989.

claim: The cell labeled in the Finlayson and Caspary study was likely a marginal cell rather than a principal cell.
source: This cell was 90–100 µm from the edge of the LSO making it likely that it is instead a marginal cell with a dendritic tree similar to two of our marginal cells illustrated in our Figure 2 (D. Caspary, personal communication, October 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on the cell's location and comparison with the authors' data, supported by personal communication.

claim: In the MSO, small somatic spikes are (along with a very large field response) a contributing factor to the well-known difficulty in recording from these cells with extracellular techniques.
source: In the MSO, small somatic spikes are (along with a very large field response) a contributing factor to the well-known difficulty in recording from these cells with extracellular techniques.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The finding that LSO principal cells have fast membranes and small action potentials suggests that these cells are also less easily isolated with extracellular techniques, compared to non-principal cells with larger overshooting spikes.
source: Our finding that LSO principal cells have fast membranes and small action potentials (Figure 4) suggests that these cells are also less easily isolated with extracellular techniques, compared to non-principal cells with larger overshooting spikes.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 4 and comparison with MSO.

claim: The small action potentials of principal cells may explain the relative paucity of onset responses and preponderance of other response types reported in LSO.
source: This may explain the relative paucity of onset responses and preponderance of other response types reported in LSO.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: The small action potentials of principal cells may necessitate close physical proximity for single-cell isolation with metal electrodes, and perhaps explains the previously reported association with injury potentials and pathology leading to underrepresented reporting of these responses in the literature.
source: Also, the small action potentials of principal cells may necessitate close physical proximity for single-cell isolation with metal electrodes, and perhaps explains the previously reported association with injury potentials and pathology leading to underrepresented reporting of these responses in the literature.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: 'Chopping' refers to regular firing where the time of occurrence of output spikes is not determined by the time of occurrence of input spikes.
source: 'Chopping' refers to regular firing where the time of occurrence of output spikes is not determined by the time of occurrence of input spikes.
evidence: This is a definition based on established knowledge.

claim: Chopping behavior has been particularly well-studied in the cochlear nucleus, where it is associated with cells that have slow membrane time constants and show poor coding of the temporal fine-structure of sounds.
source: This behavior has been particularly well-studied in the cochlear nucleus, where it is associated with cells that have slow membrane time constants and show poor coding of the temporal fine-structure of sounds (Young and Oertel, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Young and Oertel, 2004.

claim: Because sound intensity is not an instantaneous property and its measurement inherently requires some temporal integration, the finding of neurons with chopper responses in a nucleus computing ILD makes computational sense.
source: Because sound intensity is not an instantaneous property and its measurement inherently requires some temporal integration, the finding of neurons with chopper responses in a nucleus computing ILD makes computational sense.
evidence: This is reasoning based on computational principles.

claim: The striking morphological and physiological specializations found in the LSO circuit, most dramatically in its inhibitory limb in the form of the calyx of Held in the MNTB, do not fit the role of ILD computation but suggest a need for temporal precision.
source: However, the striking morphological and physiological specializations that are found in this circuit, most dramatically in its inhibitory limb in the form of the calyx of Held in the MNTB (Figure 1A), do not fit the role of ILD computation but suggest a need for temporal precision (Joris and Yin, 1995).
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical and physiological features and supported by citation to Joris and Yin, 1995.

claim: Spherical bushy and MNTB principal cells primarily receive very large individual suprathreshold somatic synapses and at high frequencies they respond very similar to sound as their inputs.
source: Spherical bushy and MNTB principal cells primarily receive very large individual suprathreshold somatic synapses and at high frequencies they respond very similar to sound as their inputs (McLaughlin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McLaughlin et al., 2008.

claim: Globular bushy cells receive many smaller subthreshold somatic and/or dendritic inputs and, as expected from their 'fast' membranes, respond reliably when the subthreshold inputs arrive at the same time, as for example at sound onset.
source: Globular bushy cells receive many smaller subthreshold somatic and/or dendritic inputs and, as expected from their 'fast' membranes, respond reliably when the subthreshold inputs arrive at the same time, as for example at sound onset.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The importance of timing in the LSO is also supported by modeling work, showing that precise temporal processing is necessary to reproduce realistic responses to amplitude-modulated sounds.
source: The importance of timing in the LSO is also supported by modeling work, showing that precise temporal processing is necessary to reproduce realistic responses to amplitude-modulated sounds (Ashida et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ashida et al., 2016.

claim: The finding that principal cells are not the temporal integrators they were thought to be, but are actually more akin to the MSO and the afferents to LSO and are triggered by fast changes in membrane potential, suggests that the LSO nucleus has a dual role: it is involved in both ILD and temporal processing.
source: Our finding that principal cells are not the temporal integrators they were thought to be, but are actually more akin to the MSO and the afferents to LSO and are triggered by fast changes in membrane potential, suggests that this nucleus has a dual role: it is involved in both ILD and temporal processing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: One promising observation is the steep sensitivity to ITDs of sound transients found in LSO.
source: The exact nature of this temporal role requires further work, but one promising observation is the steep sensitivity to ITDs of sound transients found in LSO (Caird and Klinke, 1983; Joris and Yin, 1995; Irvine et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Caird and Klinke, 1983; Joris and Yin, 1995; Irvine et al., 2001.

claim: The data suggests that the temporal precision of LSO neurons can contribute to their ILD tuning, because the latency of postsynaptic potentials decreases when stimulus intensity increases.
source: Our data also suggests that the temporal precision of LSO neurons can contribute to their ILD tuning, because the latency of postsynaptic potentials decreases when stimulus intensity increases (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Time-intensity trading has been described in in vitro and in vivo studies from the LSO and other binaural nuclei, especially for transient stimuli.
source: Such time-intensity trading has been described in in vitro (Sanes, 1990) and in vivo studies from the LSO and other binaural nuclei, especially for transient stimuli (Pollak, 1988; Irvine et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sanes, 1990; Pollak, 1988; Irvine et al., 2001.

claim: The finding of fast membrane features in LSO principal cells suggests that discrepancies in the in vitro literature are based on the lack of cell identification.
source: Our finding of fast membrane features in LSO principal cells suggests that discrepancies in the in vitro literature are based on the lack of cell identification.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and comparison with the in vitro literature.

claim: Two studies using mouse and/or gerbil slices indicated that, similar to the authors' observations, virtually all LSO principal cells in both species responded to depolarizing current steps with an onset response.
source: Two studies using mouse and/or gerbil slices (Hassfurth et al., 2009; Walcher et al., 2011) indicated that, similar to our observations, virtually all LSO principal cells in both species responded to depolarizing current steps with an onset response.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hassfurth et al., 2009; Walcher et al., 2011.

claim: Hassfurth et al. and Walcher et al. suggested that other non-onset responses from LSO cells described in other reports were due to the young age of the animals used, varying ACSF/electrode solutions and unnatural bath temperatures.
source: They suggested that other non-onset responses from LSO cells described in other reports (see below) were due to the young age of the animals used, varying ACSF/electrode solutions and unnatural bath temperatures.
evidence: This is based on citations to Hassfurth et al., 2009; Walcher et al., 2011.

claim: It is also possible that some of the recordings in other in vitro reports were from non-principal cells because in most cases the cells were not identified anatomically and many of the cells described had overshooting action potentials, a feature that in the authors' data is confined to non-principal cells.
source: It is, however, also possible that some of the recordings in these reports were from non-principal cells because in most cases the cells were not identified anatomically (Sanes, 1990; Wu and Kelly, 1994; Kandler and Friauf, 1995; Sterenborg et al., 2010; Kotak and Sanes, 2014; Remme et al., 2014) and many of the cells described had overshooting action potentials, a feature that in our data is confined to non-principal cells.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings and comparison with the in vitro literature.

claim: Spatial gradients along the tonotopic axis of LSO have been brought forward as another factor contributing to discrepancies in the in vitro literature.
source: Another factor that has been brought forward are spatial gradients, along the tonotopic axis of LSO (Koch and Sanes, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Koch and Sanes, 1998.

claim: Remme et al. describe in vitro data showing faster membrane properties for cells in the lateral, low frequency, limb of the LSO than for cells in the medial, high frequency, limb of the LSO.
source: For example, Remme et al. describe in vitro data showing faster membrane properties for cells in the lateral, low frequency, limb of the LSO than for cells in the medial, high frequency, limb of the LSO (Remme et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Remme et al., 2014.

claim: Many of the slower cells in the Remme et al. study were located near the nucleus edge, supporting the hypothesis that these are marginal cells.
source: Many of the slower cells were located near the nucleus edge (their Figure 2B), supporting the hypothesis that these are marginal cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on citation to Remme et al., 2014 and the authors' findings.

claim: The authors' in vivo finding of onset responses in confirmed principal cells necessitates a reappraisal of the in vitro studies.
source: Our in vivo finding of onset responses in confirmed principal cells necessitates a reappraisal of the in vitro studies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: The authors hypothesize that the presence of multiple cell types combined with various (unavoidable) sampling biases has led to discrepancies in the in vitro literature, and that it can be resolved by identification of the cells recorded from.
source: We hypothesize that the presence of multiple cell types combined with various (unavoidable) sampling biases has led to discrepancies in that literature, and that it can be resolved by identification of the cells recorded from.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings and comparison with the literature.

claim: Most of the authors' labeled LSO neurons were localized in the most ventral part of the nucleus, which is a consequence of the experimental approach.
source: Most of our labeled LSO neurons were localized in the most ventral part of the nucleus, which is a consequence of the experimental approach
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental observations and their explanation.

claim: The experimental approach explains the paucity of very low and high-CF cells in the authors' sample.
source: This explains the paucity of very low and high-CF cells in our sample.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental approach.

claim: The sampling bias probably also led to the relatively large proportion of marginal cells and small proportion of principal cells in the authors' sample compared to that of Helfert and Schwartz.
source: This issue probably also led to the relatively large proportion of marginal cells and small proportion of principal cells in our sample compared to that of Helfert and Schwartz (Figure 3).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental approach and comparison with Helfert and Schwartz.

claim: The results contribute to an emerging picture of the auditory brainstem composed of parallel circuits operating at different time scales.
source: At a broader level, our results contribute to an emerging picture of the auditory brainstem composed of parallel circuits operating at different time scales.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and their broader implications.

claim: The presence of multiple types of projection neurons extracting different cues from the auditory nerve, including different temporal features (fine-structure, envelopes, transients), has been a longstanding theme in the cochlear nucleus.
source: The presence of multiple types of projection neurons extracting different cues from the auditory nerve, including different temporal features (fine-structure, envelopes, transients), has been a longstanding theme in the cochlear nucleus (Young and Oertel, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Young and Oertel, 2004.

claim: Recent work, including the present results, suggests that even within the different circuits originating in the cochlear nucleus and ultimately feeding into the midbrain, subcircuits are embedded that repeat the theme of using the same afferent inputs towards different computations.
source: Recent work, including the present results, suggests that even within the different circuits originating in the cochlear nucleus and ultimately feeding into the midbrain, subcircuits are embedded that repeat the theme of using the same afferent inputs towards different computations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and recent work in the field.

claim: Psychophysics-based models also suggest several operational time scales that differ strikingly between perceptual tasks in both monaural and binaural hearing.
source: Interestingly, psychophysics-based models also suggest several operational time scales that differ strikingly between perceptual tasks in both monaural and binaural hearing (Viemeister and Plack, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Viemeister and Plack, 1993.

claim: Further probing of the binaural sensitivity of different cell groups within and across nuclei with regard to time scale of integration, and relating this to behavioral sensitivity promises a better understanding of their mutual relationship.
source: Further probing of the binaural sensitivity of different cell groups within and across nuclei with regard to time scale of integration, and relating this to behavioral sensitivity promises a better understanding of their mutual relationship (Brown and Tollin, 2016).
evidence: This is speculation about future research directions, supported by citation to Brown and Tollin, 2016.
